page.title: Mayhem Encyclopedia Custom Articles
page.t:
You begin your journey in the outer border galaxies - regions shaped by two great conflicts that defined the modern era.

Centuries ago, the Terraformers were corrupted when terraformer scientist Martin Winters altered their termination protocols. The machines abandoned their mandate to build worlds and began exterminating biological life. The resulting First Terraformer Conflict saw the Terrans fight for survival against their own creations - the machines now known as the Xenon.

In the centuries that followed, tensions between the Terrans and the Commonwealth escalated into a series of wars. After five major conflicts, the Commonwealth - Argon, Boron, Paranid, Split, and Teladi - was expelled from the Terran core systems and permitted to settle only in the frontier sectors. These outer regions were placed under the authority of Terracorp, a powerful Terran corporation tasked with managing what became known as "external affairs."

The border galaxies remain unstable. Xenon forces persist in significant numbers, internal rivalries divide the Commonwealth, and the Terrans maintain only a limited expeditionary presence.

Whether you stand with the exiled factions, serve Terran interests, or arise from the machine legacy of the original catastrophe, you begin as a minor actor in a divided frontier - where power is fragile and history is written by the victors.

The following text is an excerpt from a book written by your father 16 years ago.

\033X... on my way here. The most important thing to remember is that history is never with us, the people. The bad guys always win and they tell their children what they want to hear. Obedience doesn't make men, free will does. You have to read between the lines and accept the truth without looking back on your actions. That's what this rebellion is about: understanding the world without fear, tears or laughter. Do you think that Terracorp pities us? Can you imagine them approving a plan that would make them less important in this galaxy? Or maybe you have been fed on sweet lies and illusions. Then let me refresh your memory on the past...

As you probably know from school, the Terrans started the terraforming of thousands of planets centuries ago. In their desperate attempt to control everything, they built an AI capable of doing the hard work, the Terraformers, which later turned against their people. What you don't know however is that the Commonwealth tried to fight the Xenon, but instead of helping them, the Terrans declared war on them because their mad scientists believed that some Xenon were still active and working in the interests of their ruthless empire.

After five consecutive wars, the Commonwealth was defeated. The Argon, Boron, Paranid, Split, and Teladi were banned from the core galaxies. For many years, they hid in the dark corners of the known universe, while the Terrans created Terracorp, a giant company intended to deal with the "outside problems". From that day, everything was made private and the Terrans managed to convince people that they were unimpeachable.

Some years later, they came up with the idea of terraforming new planets... They didn't realize how strong the Xenon had become over time, and Terracorp stole billions of credits in taxes to send Terrans to their death against these vicious machines. But then, the desire for more profits made them change their minds. Instead of sending more military ships to the galaxies controlled by the Xenon, they auctioned these sectors to the remnants of the Commonwealth, making them believe that they could rise again and become the strong factions they always wanted to be. The core sectors would still be closed to them, and they would always remain at the edge of the conquered universe, but they were free to exist and they wouldn't have to hide anymore. They accepted the offer and bought hundreds of galaxies infested with Xenon. Of course, this threat was hidden from them by the Terrans. What they did tell them, however, was that Terracorp was in charge of these outer border galaxies. Some rules were designed to limit the expansion of each faction. Obviously, this led to internal wars, and without leaders able to reunite everyone, we stood no chance against the Terrans. We had to deal with the cupidity and the thirst for power on one side, and the Xenon on the other side...

End of the excerpt.

Each sector has several statistics, which are displayed in its description on your galaxy map and in the Ministry of War menu:

Population: The maximum population supported by an Outpost in this sector. Population also contributes to your global supply cap. For more information, see Empire -> Supply.

Research Rate: Determines the speed of a Research station in this sector. It also affects Hacking stations and the Cyberwar Center perk.

Station Support: The maximum number of stations allowed in this sector. This includes all docks and factories except Pirate Bases, Company stations, and the Stock Exchange.

De Jure Owner: The faction that considers this sector part of its rightful territory. AI factions place significantly more value on sectors where they are the de jure owner when deciding where to invade. De jure sectors cannot be bought, but they can be conquered.

Company: If a Company is assigned to a safe sector, it will establish a Trading Station there. The wares traded depend on the Company.

Abnormal Signals: Stronger signals attract certain dangerous threats. They reduce the cost of OCV ships built in the sector and accelerate OCV ship conversion.

Terran Memory: Indicates that debris and wreckage remain from earlier Terran attempts to terraform this region. Research stations can use these remnants to study Terran technologies. The Terran empire is considered the de jure owner of all Terran Memory sectors.

Outpost Production and Consumption: Determines which type of food an Outpost in this sector produces and which type it consumes.

The economy is focused on production and crafting. The number of resources has been reduced, and prices and profit margins are generally much lower than in the base game.

Resources transported throughout the galaxy have a purpose. They are consumed by Outposts to build ships, station kits, and equipment, or by factories to manufacture higher-tier products.

Ships are built by Outposts rather than artificially spawned. When a faction builds a ship, it must pay for that ship using actual resources from its economy.

The galaxy is divided between several competing powers.

The six major powers - Argon, Boron, Paranid, Split, Teladi, and Terran - control established territories and wage conventional wars for expansion.

Several machine factions emerged from the Terraformer catastrophe. The Xenon form the widespread territorial presence of the Terraformer network, while the more advanced OCV serve as its highly aggressive offensive branch. Phanon is a rogue Terraformer intelligence whose objectives may align with or oppose the player.

Independent and irregular forces also operate throughout the frontier. The Renegades are decentralized warbands that exploit instability and overextension, while the Yaki operate as a criminal organization. For more information about the Renegades, see Mechanics -> Renegades.

Each major faction begins with its own territory and will attempt to conquer additional sectors. For more details, see Warfare -> Invasions and Warfare -> Squadrons.

If you are coming from Litcube's Universe \(LU\), note that Phanon has been reimagined as a rogue Terraformer faction rather than a corporation. The OCV has also been completely reimagined and does not follow its LU behavior. Both the Xenon and OCV can conquer sectors.

Companies are minor factions that remain neutral in the wars fought throughout the galaxy. Each Company operates its own Trading Stations, which trade different wares depending on the Company. Their Traders can operate safely despite hostilities between other factions. Companies also employ mercenaries that you can hire through your Personal Console.

Companies are sector-based and will establish a Trading Station only when their assigned sector is safe - that is, when it is neither Unknown nor controlled by the Xenon. Unless you have joined the OCV, any sector you own is considered safe.

Destroying Company assets is illegal. Destroying their stations results in reputation loss, while destroying their Traders increases your infamy.

To expand your empire, deploy an Outpost or a factory in an unclaimed sector to conquer it. To conquer a sector owned by another faction, you must first destroy all of its stations except Company stations and Pirate Bases. Conquering a sector also costs reputation with adjacent factions, except for your first sector. Be careful when expanding near other factions, as the reputation loss can turn a neighbor hostile.

Through your Personal Console, you can abandon a sector you own or offer to transfer it to another faction, as long as you are not hostile to that faction. The faction may decline the offer. Transferring a sector grants 1 Favor Point, plus 1 additional Favor Point for every 2 terraformed planets in that sector. No Favor Points are awarded if the sector was transferred in response to an ultimatum.

On harder difficulties, factions may issue an ultimatum demanding one of your sectors. You have 1 hour to transfer the demanded sector to that faction. Missing the deadline, abandoning the sector, or transferring it to another faction counts as a refusal and results in a war declaration.

Don't expand too quickly! Each new sector can attract the attention of Xenon or Pirates. Make sure you have enough firepower to defend your existing territory before pushing deeper into the frontier.

In addition to conquering unclaimed sectors by building a station in them, you can also purchase sectors from your origin faction. This feature is unavailable as a Xenon Defect. Purchasing a sector requires sufficient money and the completion of several missions in that sector.

Factions will not sell all of their territory. Only their cheapest sectors and sectors under your influence, such as those adjacent to your territory, can be purchased. De jure sectors are never sold, and weak empires will not sell any sectors.

When you purchase a sector, you gain ownership of all stations within it, including the Outpost if present. Each sector you purchase increases the cost of future purchases.

Outposts are the main stations of every faction, including yours. They serve as local headquarters and production centers capable of building ships, station kits, lasers, missiles, and equipment.

Outposts require people and resources to operate. You must provide food to prevent the population from starving. Each Outpost produces one type of food and consumes another, depending on its sector \(see Sector Stats\). Food consumption can be removed with the No Food Consumption perk.

When a new Outpost is built, it receives an initial population of 40 people at the start of the next Outpost consumption cycle \(10 minutes\), provided there is enough food. The initial population is granted only once. Afterward, the population grows naturally by up to 9 people per cycle \(default growth rate\), with growth slowing as the Outpost approaches its population limit. Population growth and other population mechanics can be modified by Outpost perks and certain faction alignments. Up to 5 people can also be transferred between Outposts.

People can work on multiple projects at the same time without any penalty. 

Outposts can be affected by various negative events. The larger an Outpost's population, the greater the chance of a negative event occurring. You can limit the maximum population of each Outpost through the Administration menu. The Insurance Policy perk can prevent these events, although harder difficulties reduce its effectiveness.

Only Traders and ships running Trade Run commands can dock at NPC Outposts. NPC Outposts will not sell Crystals, Hull Plating, Computer Components, Quantum Tubes, or Silicon Wafers, as these are reserved for shipbuilding.

An Outpost can be upgraded to a Capital Shipyard. The upgrade costs Outposts, Blue Crystals, and Green Crystals, with the cost depending on difficulty. A Capital Shipyard provides 10% more ship specialization, 2 additional perk slots, a 1.2x recycling factor, and additional capital ship docking slots.

Crafting is one of the core features of Mayhem. Ships, station kits, lasers, missiles, and equipment can be crafted using resources. In Mayhem, Saturn Complex Hubs and Vanilla Complexes are disabled, and production costs have been adjusted accordingly.

Crafting costs are based on the average price of the product and the resources required to produce it.

Each Outpost has separate specialization levels for ships, lasers, missiles, and stations. Completing projects in a specific category increases its specialization, reducing both research and production time. Specialization has diminishing returns.

By default, base specialization ranges from 0% to 20%. It can be further increased through terraforming effects and Terraforming efficiency 4, a milestone perk. Specific specializations can also be increased through the Cheaper stations perk, Renegades plot completion, and the Capital Shipyard. AI factions use dynamic specialization.

Cancelling a project always refunds all invested resources.

Crafting ships requires population.

All ships are built with a default set of shields and lasers. Creating additional lasers is optional and allows you to customize ship loadouts.

Mobile Factories provide an alternative form of production, although mobile production is less efficient than using normal factories. Mobile Factory Kits can be crafted through Hangar -> Upgrade Ship at an Outpost. A Mobile Factory Kit can be equipped to either a Kha'ak ship or an ST-cargo ship. On Normal difficulty and above, the number of Mobile Factories you can operate at once is limited based on the number of planets in your empire. On Easy, this limit applies only if the Mobile Factory limit modifier is enabled.

Workers are automated ships that help run your empire. Each Outpost and some factories have a limited number of Worker slots for different Worker types. You can view these limits and other Worker settings in the Administration tab of your Outposts.

Agents: Agents can operate from an Outpost or factory. At an Outpost, they perform jobs from the list configured in the Outpost Manager's Logistics menu. At a factory, they import resources and export products between your stations. Unlike Traders, Agents never trade with stations you do not own. Agents and Traders are synchronized with each other.

Explorers: Explorers ensure that every reachable sector is monitored by an Advanced Satellite. If no Advanced Satellites are available from your stations, they will wait until one becomes available. They do not purchase Satellites from other factions. Unlike other Workers, Explorers have a fixed range of 15 sectors and ignore the "Max. sector distance for all Workers" setting.

Looters: Looters search reachable sectors for abandoned wares and return them to their homebase.

Miners: Miners assigned to an Outpost or a Quantum Tube Fab mine debris in its sector and unload their cargo at their homebase when full. Mobile mining fleets no longer exist. Only Ore, Silicon Wafers, colored crystals, and minerals can be mined. Crystals and minerals can be sold or used to craft equipment through your Outposts' hangars.

Traders: Sector Traders \(ST\) and Universal Traders \(UT\) no longer exist. Traders are the only Workers that can trade with factories you do not own. Other factions can also send Traders to your Outposts if you allow them. Traders and Agents coordinate their jobs by "locking" wares at their destinations, preventing multiple Workers from making the same trip for the same ware.

Tugs: Tugs search reachable sectors for abandoned ships and return them to their homebase. Some mission and special ships, such as ships emitting a remnant signal, cannot be captured by Tugs.

The AI uses the same Workers and scripts. However, the AI also uses Service ships for flavor. Service ships have no gameplay effect.

All Workers except Explorers respect their homebase's "Max. sector distance for all Workers" setting. For performance reasons, Agents and Traders have a maximum range of 8 sectors. This limit can be changed in the configuration files.

Two main screens are used to manage logistics: Agents and Traders. Both are found in the Logistics tab of the Outpost Manager.

Agents manage only your stations. To trade with stations owned by other factions, you need Traders. Wares that Traders can import or export through your Outposts must be manually added to the Traders list.

Each factory has import and export thresholds that can be configured through its Station Parameters menu. Agents and Traders check these thresholds before departure and, for exports, again upon arrival.

Each Outpost and factory can be configured to allow or forbid your Traders and NPC Traders. When you build your first Outpost, allowing NPC Traders to dock can help you acquire necessary resources, especially food.

When an AI Trader visits one of your stations, it can buy products or sell resources. If the station does not have enough money to purchase all of the Trader's wares, you will be notified. Credits will not be taken from your main account to cover the difference.

AI Traders will not trade at any price. Their tolerance for unfavorable prices depends on your Trade Rank. Factories have an Automatic Pricing setting, which is recommended for most situations.

Traders coordinate their jobs by "locking" their destinations, preventing multiple Traders from making the same trip for the same ware.

Each station has a "Max. sector distance for all Workers" setting. This determines how far Agents and Traders will search for trading partners and also affects most other Workers. The "Reachable Factories" job setting also uses this range.

Station parameters can be modified through either the vanilla station menu or the Station Settings menu in your Personal Console. Automatic credit transfers can be configured only through the Station Settings menu.

Logistics is one of the most complex aspects of Mayhem because of its flexibility and the amount of control it provides. This example demonstrates how to set up a production chain for Teladianium, Rastar Oil, and Ore, the materials required for station construction.

You will need:

- Any sector. All sectors can support at least 8 stations.
- 4 TS-class ships to use as Agents. They can be slow and inexpensive, as they do not need to leave the sector.
- An Outpost to build the ships and craft the required station kits.

Your first Outpost provides enough starting resources to build the stations required for this production chain:

- Chelt Space Aquarium: Produces Chelts Meat from Energy Cells.
- Chemical Lab: Produces Chemicals from Waste. Waste is automatically produced by Outposts.
- Food Preparation Facility: Produces C-Ration from Protein Paste.
- Ore Mine: Produces Ore from C-Ration. You can also use Miners to collect Ore and Silicon Wafers.
- Protein Paste Blending Facility: Produces Protein Paste from Waste.
- Rastar Refinery: Produces Rastar Oil from Chelts Meat.
- Teladianium Foundry: Produces Teladianium from Chemicals.

Once the stations are built, open the Logistics menu and configure these jobs:

- Import Teladianium from local factories. The most expensive factory requires around 4,500 Teladianium.
- Import Ore from local factories. The most expensive factory requires around 7,500 Ore.
- Export Energy Cells to local factories. This assumes you have the Solar panels perk. Otherwise, Energy Cells can be purchased from other factions using a Trader or produced by a Solar Power Plant if the sector has enough Station Support.
- Export Waste to local factories.

One simple approach is to assign 1 Agent each to the Outpost, Food Preparation Facility, Rastar Refinery, and Teladianium Foundry. Factory Agents handle both imports and exports. For example, the Food Preparation Facility's Agent imports Protein Paste and exports C-Ration to the Ore Mine. The Rastar Refinery's Agent imports Chelts Meat and exports the finished Rastar Oil to your Outpost.

A more scalable approach is to assign multiple Agents to the Outpost and use it as the logistics hub. As a rule of thumb, 1 Agent can support approximately 2-3 factories. Add these jobs to the Outpost's Logistics menu:

- Import Chemicals from local factories.
- Import Chelts Meat from local factories.
- Import Protein Paste from local factories.
- Import C-Ration from local factories.
- Export Chemicals to local factories.
- Export Chelts Meat to local factories.
- Export C-Ration to local factories.
- Export Protein Paste to local factories.

With this setup, the Outpost acts as the central logistics hub. Agents distribute basic and intermediate resources from the Outpost to your factories and return finished products to the Outpost.

If you still have Station Support available, consider building an Advanced Satellite Factory. Advanced Satellites require only Energy Cells, can supply an Explorer, and can also be sold for a good price.

If you need additional production but have no free station slots, an ST-cargo ship equipped with a Mobile Factory Kit can provide additional production. For more information about Mobile Factories and their empire-wide limit, see the Manufacture section.

Research allows you to unlock ship blueprints so they can be built at your Outposts. Blueprints are listed at Research stations and in the Blueprints menu of your Personal Console. There are four ways to gain research toward a blueprint.

The first way is to scan ships. Scanning requires the Data Scanner you receive at game start \(inventory item\) and its associated hotkey. Scanning a ship is free and safe, but provides only a small amount of research. Larger ships may require multiple scans of several ships of the same type to unlock their blueprint.

The second and much faster way is to use Research stations. These stations can study ships to unlock their blueprints for use by all your Outposts. Each sector has a different Research Rate, so choosing a good sector is important. Research projects can be interrupted and resumed at any time and do not require population. Terran ships can be researched only in sectors with Terran Memory \(see the Universe Map\).

The third way is to successfully board a ship. The first successful boarding of a ship type grants up to the first 25% of its blueprint.

The fourth way is to recycle ships. For most ships, the amount of research gained depends on your current blueprint progress:

- 0-25% researched: gain 40%.
- 26-50% researched: gain 25%.
- 51-85% researched: gain 10%.

Recycling can normally provide research only up to 85%. The remaining 15% must be completed using the Data Scanner or Research stations.

Recycling has two exceptions:

- Advanced and prototype ships can unlock only the first 50% and 70% of their blueprints through recycling, respectively.
- OCV ships cannot be recycled once their blueprint has reached at least 85% research.

Plot progression can unlock blueprints directly, bypassing the normal research process. Joining the OCV disables research entirely but grants guaranteed blueprints instead.

Supply determines how many ships your empire can support. You start with a base amount of supply determined by difficulty.

A sector must have an Outpost to generate supply. Each Outpost provides supply equal to 5 times its maximum population.

Your total supply is equal to your starting supply plus the supply generated by your Outposts. You can increase your supply by expanding into additional sectors or terraforming planets. Most terraformed planets increase the sector's population through their generic terraforming bonus, which increases the Outpost's maximum population and the supply it generates.

Every ship you own consumes supply. In general, larger and more powerful ships require more supply than smaller ones. Xenon ships consume 25% less supply, while OCV ships consume 50% more. Stations and other infrastructure do not consume supply; only ships contribute to supply usage.

If your fleet's supply usage exceeds your available supply, ship construction and maintenance costs increase proportionally to how far you exceed the limit. Other factions will also respond to your overextension. You can reduce supply usage by recycling ships or losing them through destruction.

Difficulty modifies your maximum supply:
- Easy: 3x
- Normal: 2x
- Hard: 1.6x
- Insane: 1x

The Maintenance menu in your Personal Console tracks the upkeep costs of your ships. Each ship has a maintenance factor that increases over time while the ship remains undocked, causing its maintenance cost to increase. A ship inspection resets its maintenance factor to 100%.

The maintenance factor does not increase if the ship is equipped with a Mobile Maintenance Kit. Ships docked at an Outpost with the Dry dock perk also incur reduced maintenance costs.

Ships not made by your origin faction normally cost 35% more maintenance. Phanon ships are exempt after completing the main plot. Private Corp. ships are always exempt, while Yaki ships are exempt if you have infamy. If you started as a Xenon Defect, Phanon ships are always exempt, while OCV ships receive only a 15% maintenance penalty instead of 35%.

Supply also affects maintenance costs. If your empire exceeds its maximum supply, maintenance costs increase according to your overextension. For more information, see the Supply section.

On harder difficulties, sectors and Jump Beacons also cost maintenance. Insane difficulty increases all maintenance costs by 50%.

Periodically, Workers are automatically repaired and maintained. Fleet followers have configurable settings for automatic repairs and maintenance.

Every Outpost can hold a limited number of perks, bought at the Outpost itself and permanent once taken.

How many it may hold is not fixed. Difficulty sets the baseline. A Capital Shipyard carries more perk slots, each planet you terraform in its sector adds one perk slot, and every faction you are in Permanent War with adds one slot to every Outpost you own, present and future. Declaring a Permanent War is therefore an economic decision as much as a diplomatic one.

One of the perks pays for itself: Adjacency Perk Bonus adds a slot for every neighboring sector where you hold an Outpost, so a solid block of territory is worth more than the same count scattered about.

Perks are where most of the comfort in the game lives: food you do not have to grow, ships that do not age while docked, faster population growth, protection from the accidents that befall a crowded Outpost.

Terraforming is unlocked as you progress through the storyline, either by helping Phanon or by joining the Xenon/OCV.

Terraforming allows you to improve planets within your sectors. Each successfully terraformed planet grants +1 Outpost perk slot and a unique planetary effect. Most terraformed planets also improve the sector's population, research, and station support stats.

Planetary effects come in four rarities: common, uncommon, anomalous, and rare.

Anomalous planets cannot initially be terraformed. Terraforming efficiency 3 is required to terraform them. Special planets may also modify or replace the normal terraforming bonuses.


Cost and Progress

Terraforming projects reduce production rates through both local and empire-wide penalties.

Terraforming progress is based on the population of the sector's Outpost and the population of adjacent Outposts.


Local Project Limit

By default, you may terraform one project at a time in a sector. This local limit can be increased by unlocking perks. The Terraforming specialist perk doubles your Outpost's terraforming manpower and increases the local limit to 3 projects.


Terraforming Efficiency

Several Outpost perks become available after terraforming enough planets:
- Terraforming efficiency 1 \(3 terraformed planets\): Increases terraforming manpower by 20%, or by 100% if you joined the OCV.
- Terraforming efficiency 2 \(7 planets\): Reduces the global terraforming penalty applied to this Outpost by 33%.
- Terraforming efficiency 3 \(12 planets\): The Outpost contributes 100% of its population to adjacent terraforming projects instead of 50%. Allows Anomalous planets to be terraformed.
- Terraforming efficiency 4 \(18 planets\): Requires the Capital Shipyard upgrade and all other Terraforming perks. Increases base max specialization by 10%.


Global Project Limit and Mastery

By default, your global limit is 1 project. For every 4 \(6 on Insane difficulty\) planets in your empire, you may terraform one additional planet at a time. After successfully terraforming your 18th planet, you master Terraforming. Mastery reduces the divisor by 1, allowing 1 additional terraforming project per 3 planets instead of 4 \(5 instead of 6 on Insane difficulty\). Having more planets also allows you to support more Mobile Factories.


Concurrent Terraforming

Terraforming multiple planets in the same sector divides the available manpower equally among all active local projects. However, completing them concurrently is still faster than completing them sequentially.

This page summarizes global ship mechanics, faction traits, sector effects, and standard equipment. These rules apply universally unless otherwise stated.

Global Ship Rules
- Building ships that can fire missiles requires the Missile manufacture perk at the Outpost.
- Xenon and OCV ignore Xenon, OCV, and Phanon ships.
- Xenon, OCV, and Phanon ships have significantly reduced crew costs.
- Xenon-aligned players pay no ship maintenance costs.
- Foreign ships cost 35% more maintenance, excluding Private Corp. ships and OWPs. Phanon ships are exempt after completing the main plot.
 - If you started as a Xenon Defect, Phanon ships are always exempt, while OCV ships receive only a 15% maintenance penalty.


Ship Traits

1. Commonwealth Races
- Boron ships: Regenerate 10% hull every 30 minutes, but generally have lower speed.
- Split ships: +20% crew cost, -3% material cost.
- Paranid ships: -20% crew cost, +3% material cost.
- Teladi ships: Weaker shields but heavier hull plating.
- Yaki ships:
 a. With infamy: -50% crew cost and exemption from the foreign maintenance penalty.
 b. Without infamy: +100% crew cost.

2. Special Factions
- Xenon ships:
 a. -50% Hull Plating
 b. -50% Computer Components
 c. -25% Supply
 d. +100% Quantum Tubes
- OCV ships:
 a. -50% Hull Plating
 b. -50% Quantum Tubes
 c. +100% Computer Components
 d. +50% Supply
- Kha'ak ships:
 a. Regenerate 5% hull every 30 minutes.
 b. Can collect any cargo, including Plasma Beam Cannons.
 c. Normally obtainable only through capture. Studying recycled Kha'ak ships may reveal their secrets.

3. Sector Effects \(OCV\)
- Higher Abnormal Signal strength reduces the material cost of OCV ships built in the sector.
- Higher Abnormal Signal strength reduces OCV ship conversion time.
- OCV ships cannot be built in sectors without Abnormal Signals.

4. Standard Ship Equipment
- Capital ships \(M1, M2, M7, TL\): Docking Computer, Triplex Scanner
- M1 and dockable M2/M7: Transporter Device, Carrier Repair Module
- M6, M8, TM: Docking Computer
- M8: CCDS MK1-MK3, Triplex Scanner
- TM: Boost Extension, Transporter Device, Carrier Repair Module

The galaxy is dynamic, and so are faction relations. The rules are as follows:

1. Factions are "Neutral" when no invasion is in progress between them or when they have signed a Truce. A Truce may be signed after a sector conquest if no further invasions are active. Truces are temporary.

2. Factions are "Friend" when bound by an Unbreakable Alliance or Coalition.

3. Factions are "Foe" when an invasion is in progress, during a Total War, or when a Permanent War exists with the player.

4. On Normal difficulty and above \(or on Easy if War Declarations are enabled in the 9973 t-file\), factions may declare war on the player.

Unbreakable Alliances and Total Wars are permanent and bound to the galaxy. They may also be triggered through special Favors.

Coalitions are temporary alliances formed by at least two minor factions against a major faction. Members of an Unbreakable Alliance or Coalition share resources.

Permanent Wars can be declared only by the player or by joining the OCV. You may declare a Permanent War against any non-coalition ally at any time. Doing so grants 1 additional perk slot to all current and future Outposts. In addition, each faction engaged in a Total War against your target grants you 1 Favor Point.

When a faction considers declaring war on you, it evaluates several factors, including its current situation, your reputation, Loyalty, infamy, supply consumption, fleet power, and whether you control any of its de jure sectors. Sharing the faction's origin and maintaining high reputation reduce the likelihood of war. Higher difficulties, controlling de jure sectors, having infamy, low fleet power, and exceeding your supply limit increase the likelihood.

Instead of immediately declaring war, a faction may issue an ultimatum demanding one of your sectors. You must own at least two sectors to receive an ultimatum; otherwise, the faction declares war immediately.

If your reputation with the faction is Rank 10 and you own at least two sectors, an ultimatum is guaranteed. Otherwise, higher reputation and Loyalty increase the chance of receiving an ultimatum instead of a war declaration.

You have 1 hour to comply with an ultimatum. Missing the deadline, abandoning the demanded sector, or transferring it to another faction counts as a refusal and results in war. However, if your reputation with the demanding faction is Rank 10 when you refuse, war is averted and your reputation is drastically reduced instead.

Each faction tracks your reputation using sixteen ranks. Many game mechanics use your reputation rank rather than the exact reputation value.

Rank -5: -1,000,000
Rank -4: -100,000
Rank -3: -10,000
Rank -2: -1,000
Rank -1: -100
Rank 0: -10
Rank 1: 10
Rank 2: 33
Rank 3: 100
Rank 4: 333
Rank 5: 1,000
Rank 6: 3,333
Rank 7: 10,000
Rank 8: 33,333
Rank 9: 100,000
Rank 10: 333,333

The scale is nonlinear. Each positive rank requires roughly three times as much reputation as the previous rank, so higher ranks take progressively longer to reach.

You are considered a close ally at rank 6 or higher \(rank 7 or higher on Insane difficulty\). Close allies can trade at the faction's Stock Exchange and receive a Police License. Falling below the required rank revokes your Police Licence.

Favor Points and Loyalty are diplomatic currencies used to influence other factions.

Favor Points can be spent in the Ministry of War to influence factions to take certain diplomatic or strategic actions. They can be purchased with Loyalty or earned directly through certain actions:

- Destroying a high-priority target \(M7-class ships marked with a *\).
- Destroying a Hive Queen spawned from a Kha'ak raid.
- Joining a Coalition.
- Transferring a sector to another faction. A transferred sector grants 1 Favor Point, plus 1 additional Favor Point for every 2 terraformed planets in that sector. No Favor Points are granted when complying with an ultimatum.

Loyalty represents assistance provided to an empire. It is earned primarily by completing missions, but it can also be earned by assisting an empire in contested territory.

Loyalty is normally used to purchase Favor Points. If the "Ship Purchase" feature is enabled in the 9972 t-file, Loyalty can also unlock the ability to purchase ships from that faction. Purchasing a ship does not consume Loyalty. Ship purchasing is always disabled on Insane difficulty.

On Normal difficulty or higher \(or on Easy with war declarations enabled in the 9973 t-file\), Loyalty also increases the chance of receiving an ultimatum instead of an immediate war declaration.

Failing or aborting a mission costs 1 Loyalty and 500 reputation. Certain deliberate mission failures, such as stealing a mission ship, double this penalty. Falling below rank 0 or going to war with a faction removes all ongoing Favors, Loyalty, and Favor Points you have with that faction.

Infamy measures how dangerous the galaxy considers you. It is separate from your reputation with individual factions.

Infamy is gained through actions such as destroying civilians, boarding ships, and breaking pacts. It gradually decreases over time, unless you have joined the OCV, in which case it does not decay.

Higher infamy makes factions more likely to move against you and makes territorial claims more difficult. While you have any infamy, factions will not sell you sectors.

Infamy also provides some benefits. Infamy enables Space Weed production. Pirates are less likely to attack your assets as your infamy increases. Yaki ships also research faster with infamy and significantly slower with none.

Invasions between other factions follow several rules:

- A faction cannot claim a sector that is already claimed.

- Claims have a limited duration, after which the invading fleet will generally retreat. Battle Groups also have a cooldown before they can claim another sector.

- Battle Groups always initiate invasions, but they can be reinforced by other fleets, such as Task Forces or Border Patrols.

- The claiming faction conquers the sector once all required stations are destroyed. Company stations and Pirate Bases are ignored.

- As the player, you automatically place a claim on a sector when you destroy one of its stations.

- When a sector becomes unclaimed after its stations are destroyed, a temporary grace period prevents unrelated factions from immediately conquering it. The grace period lasts 2.5 hours on Easy, 2 hours on Normal, 1.5 hours on Hard, and 1 hour on Insane. During this period, the player and the faction responsible for its abandonment may still conquer the sector. Once the grace period expires, other factions may conquer it normally.

- Xenon and OCV do not place normal claims. If a Xenon or OCV invasion is already contesting a sector when its final required station is destroyed, the Terraformers conquer the sector instead of leaving it unclaimed.

- Any faction can be completely annihilated.

To defend their territories, invade new sectors and harass their enemies, the major factions operate several types of fleets:

Battle Group: Used to invade and conquer sectors. Battle Groups generally regroup at a safe location before placing a claim, then advance toward their target.

Border Patrol: Defends border sectors, prioritizing "hot sectors" \(see below\).

Escort: Usually escorts civilian ships \(Workers\). Otherwise, it defends its current sector.

Police: Pursues ships carrying illegal wares and may attack hostile ships in adjacent sectors. Otherwise, it defends its current sector.

Rearguard: Functions like a Border Patrol but focuses on non-border sectors.

Task Force: The most aggressive fleet type. Task Forces can enter hostile territory to attack random ships even when their faction is not at war with the target. They prioritize destroying enemy satellites and Jump Beacons and assisting Battle Groups.

Raider: A fleet of roughly a dozen fast M3/M4-class fighters that conducts deep raids against enemy logistics during wartime. Raiders penetrate hostile territory and target TS-class transports when possible. When raiding your empire, they also target TP-class transports. On harder difficulties, Raiders are more likely to target your empire instead of other factions.

Factions use an Alert system. When a ship is attacked or another dangerous event occurs, an Alert is raised and the affected sector becomes "hot" for a short time. Hot sectors receive increased attention from most fleets.

Most fleets will retreat when they consider themselves overwhelmed. They will travel to the nearest safe Outpost and wait for reinforcements.

Missiles have been completely overhauled to reduce confusion between missile types and create a more believable combat model.

There are four missile categories:

- Fox 1: Semi-active radar homing missiles. These missiles require a locked target before firing. They are relatively slow and have medium range. Only CCDS MK1 can identify Fox 1 missiles. Identification can occur at long range and is required before chaff can be deployed.

- Fox 2: Infrared homing missiles. These missiles do not require a target lock and can even track other missiles. They are fast and short-ranged, but they are less effective against ships with small heat signatures, such as fighters. Only CCDS MK2 can identify Fox 2 missiles, and only at medium range.

- Fox 3: Active radar homing missiles. These missiles do not require a target lock and combine high speed with long range. Only CCDS MK3 can identify Fox 3 missiles, and only at short range.

- Artillery missiles: Passive radar homing missiles designed for specialized missile platforms. They have the highest speed, range, damage, and price of all missile types. Due to their unstable nature, artillery missiles cannot be intercepted by CCDS and chaff. Like other missiles, however, they can still be destroyed by laser fire, although missiles are much more durable than in vanilla.

Every faction has access to missiles from the Fox categories, while artillery missiles are limited to specialized factions and ships.

The AI has been improved to use missiles efficiently while maintaining performance and balance. NPC ships generally do not use missiles during out-of-sector combat and avoid firing them at small fighters. Player-owned ships can still use missiles out-of-sector. M8 bombers and M7M missile frigates are an exception for the AI and can also launch missiles during out-of-sector combat. Each M8 has built-in CCDS with extended missile detection range, allowing it to protect nearby allies from incoming missiles.

Fighters cannot fire missiles. Only M1, M2, M6, M7, M7M, and M8-class ships can use them. Artillery missiles are normally exclusive to M7M frigates, although certain specialized ships may also use them. All other missile-capable classes can use Fox missiles.

Chaff cannot be deployed manually. CCDS already has an extremely low failure rate, and no pilot can react faster than a targeting computer.

Hacking allows you to disrupt, damage, or capture ships. To begin hacking, you need three things:

- A Hacking Rootkit: Gives you access to Hacking commands through your ship console. These commands are available only from the ship you are personally flying.
- Hackerchips: Required to install or remove a backdoor on a vulnerable target. Hackerchips can be produced at an Outpost, periodically through the Cyberwar Center perk, or with a Mobile Factory. Outpost production costs twice as much as Mobile Factory production.
- A Hacking station: A Research station can be converted into a Hacking station by purchasing the appropriate perk at its local Outpost. Hacking stations are used to research vulnerabilities and create viruses.

Once you have these requirements, the first step is to identify vulnerable ports. Scan a target using Hacking -> Scan Target Ports, or use an Outpost with the Cyberwar Center perk to periodically open ports for you. Discovered ports can be reviewed through Hacking -> Show Database Entry. Each port provides access to one of the target's systems:

- Accounting: Steals money from the target's bank account. If you have joined the OCV, the target drops a crate of Red Crystals instead.
- Cargo: Forces the target to drop part of its cargo.
- Hull Cooling: Damages the target's hull.
- Navigation: Temporarily disrupts the target's controls, forcing it to move randomly between adjacent sectors.
- Oxygen: Kills the crew, allowing the ship to be captured.
- Shields: Causes a temporary power outage affecting both the target's laser and shield generators.
- Weapons: Temporarily disables the target's weapon systems.

The second step is to install a backdoor on one of the target's open ports:

- Closed: Cannot be hacked.
- Secured: Can be opened by spending research on the port.
- Open: Can have a backdoor installed at the cost of 1 Hackerchip.
- Patched: Previously compromised and temporarily unavailable for hacking.

Researching a secured port costs both time and money. Unlike Research stations, Hacking stations require funds to be deposited before research can begin. If you have joined the OCV, Hacking stations consume Red Crystals stored at their local Outpost instead of money.

Ships equipped with Advanced Firewall Software have all their ports closed and cannot be hacked.

Installing a backdoor does not immediately alert the target, but the vulnerability may eventually be detected. If this happens, the port becomes patched and remains unavailable for hacking for a long time.

Once you have installed a backdoor on a target, the target becomes vulnerable and you can inject a virus into its systems. A virus affects only one system on one vector, but it can affect multiple targets at once. Targeting the same system through a different vector requires another virus.

When creating a virus, you can prioritize efficiency or security. This choice affects several properties, most notably the maximum range from the Hacking station at which the virus can be dispatched. Targets outside this range cannot be hacked.

Once the virus is ready, you can dispatch it to targets within range:

1. Select one or more targets. The virus will affect the system it was designed to target on each selected ship.
2. Select relays. A relay is a reachable ship on which you have installed a backdoor. It acts as a proxy, making it more difficult for a backtrace to reach you.
3. Confirm and dispatch the virus. The virus takes time to infect the targeted systems and take effect. You will be notified when this occurs.

Targets have different numbers of nodes depending on their size. The more nodes a target has, the longer the virus takes to infect its system. Each node also provides another opportunity for the attack to be backtraced. Backtrace checks are performed at each relay, and a backtrace must successfully pass through every relay before reaching your Hacking station and identifying you as the attacker.

If you are successfully backtraced while you have no infamy, you gain 1 infamy but are not counterattacked. If you already have infamy, the target faction instead launches a cyber counterattack against several of your ships. These counterattacks can affect your ships in the same ways your viruses affect their targets.

Quickhacking provides an alternative approach. No Outpost perks are required; all you need is a ship with a Hacking Rootkit and 1 Hackerchip. Quickhacks have a random efficiency between 30% and 70% and take effect immediately. However, they cannot target the Oxygen and Accounting systems and are always traced back to you. After a quickhack, the targeted system is immediately patched for the entire ship line, while all other ports on the quickhacked ship are closed.

Boarding is largely unchanged from vanilla. To begin a boarding operation, you need marines, Boarding Pods, and a ship capable of launching them. Most M6, M8, and capital ships can launch Boarding Pods.

Pirate Bases are especially useful for early boarding operations. They sell Boarding Pods and more skilled marines.

Your Outposts can provide the resources needed for further boarding operations. Boarding Pods can be crafted at an Outpost, while marines can be recruited once the Outpost reaches at least 75% of its maximum population. Outpost recruits begin with low skill levels but are capable of boarding M6 and TM-class ships, provided at least two surviving marines have sufficient Hacking skill during the final stage. The Pirate contract perk increases their initial Fighting skill. Alternatively, joining the OCV during the main plot provides improved recruits.

Boarding ships costs reputation and may also increase your infamy.

Unlike vanilla, ships can have more internal defenses. Most M6 and TM-class ships have none, except mercenary ships, which always have all three types. Capital ships have a chance to spawn with internal defenses, and these chances are doubled on Insane difficulty. Xenon and OCV ships are guaranteed to have internal defenses.

After successfully hacking the core, the enemy crew makes one final stand. This stage is independent of your marines' Fighting skill and depends only on how many marines survived the hacking stage. The more surviving marines you have, the more additional losses you will incur.

If the boarded ship had a bounty or was a Renegade roamer, you receive the same rewards as if you had destroyed it. Boarding a Renegade roamer awards more crystals than destroying it. If it had any lasers and followers when captured, issuing it an attack command will cause those followers to come under your control.

Several hotkeys provide access to important Mayhem features. The Personal Console is the menu you will use most frequently. It can be accessed through its hotkey or through the Additional Ship Commands menu on your ships. Note that all custom hotkeys are disabled while you are docked due to a hardcoded limitation.

Many gameplay variables can be changed through two configuration files: X3/addon/t/9972-L044.xml and X3/addon/t/9973-L044.xml.\n\nThese files allow many aspects of the game to be customized and are often referred to as "t-files."

Difficulty is selected during the initial survey and cannot be changed afterward. It affects:

- The strength of Xenon and OCV invasions, wandering Xenon fleets, and Renegade ships.
- The number of Xenon stations in each sector, and therefore the strength of their defensive forces. 
- The number of pirates spawned from Pirate Bases.
- The chance for Pirate Bases to spawn in unclaimed sectors.

Higher difficulties introduce additional player limitations and more aggressive NPC behavior, including:

- More difficult missions.
- Fewer free sectors after conquering your first sector.
- Fewer perk slots available at each Outpost.
- Additional perks used by NPC Outposts.
- Increased chance of NPC war declarations.
- Fewer lasers and shields retained by bailed ships.
- Shorter black market ship timers.
- Reduced tax income.

See the Insane Difficulty section for the full list of modifiers.

Insane difficulty adds additional constraints and scaling on top of Hard:

1. Starting Conditions
- After you conquer your first sector, all remaining unclaimed sectors are immediately conquered by other factions, severely limiting further expansion opportunities.
- Nation status is granted after acquiring a sector or completing 1/3 of one of the required milestones.
- Ascension:
 - Quickstart is disabled.
 - Standard ascension is replaced with a special version featuring higher quotas and randomized tasks.
- No starting bonus ships, credits, or revealed sectors. Your starting ship's blueprint is not automatically unlocked.
- No starting reputation bonus with your origin faction. Start with an additional -1000 reputation with all other Commonwealth factions.
- The Maelstrom \(OCV portal\) is placed in a random Xenon sector, and its location is not revealed at the start.

2. Player Limitations
- Reduced tutorial guidance.

- Economy and Progression:
 - Maintenance costs increased by 50%.
 - Tax income reduced by 50%.
 - Boarding and Trade Union rewards reduced by 33%.
 - Recycle efficiency reduced by 20%.
 - Renegade roamers drop 33% fewer crystals.
 - Reduced chance of missions that reward ships.

- Logistics and Access:
 - TS and TP restrictions:
 - Black market prices for TS and TP-class ships are 10 times higher.
 - TS and TP research and blueprints are unavailable, except from main plot rewards.
 - Capital Shipyard:
 - More expensive.
 - Required to build M7, M2, and M1-class ships.

- Intel and Control:
 - Police Licenses, placing or capturing Jump Beacons, and maintaining deployables \(Jump Beacons and satellites\) in NPC sectors require at least rank 7 reputation.
 - Satellite cleanup is always enabled.
 - Infamy benefits are reduced.

- Systems and Mobility:
 - Terraforming penalties are increased.
 - The global project and Mobile Factory limits are reduced.
 - Teleportation requires a Transporter Device on the target ship.
 - The Jump Point limit is reduced by 25%.
 - Favor and OCV conversion timers are reduced by 30%.

3. NPC Behavior

- Combat and Equipment:
 - Reduced ship bail chance. Bailed ships retain even fewer lasers and shields.
 - NPC capital ships are more likely to spawn with internal defenses.
 - All TS and TP-class ships have a 50% chance to spawn with Advanced Firewall Software.

- Scaling and Aggression:
 - NPC factions are more aggressive, better equipped, and scale their fleets more aggressively in response to your fleet strength.
 - NPC factions are less likely to issue ultimatums and can declare war without a shared border.
 - Raider fleets are more likely to target your empire.

- Expansion and Systems:
 - Explorers have a 1% chance to conquer unclaimed sectors \(vs. 0.2% on Hard\).
 - Xenon infect Jump Beacons faster.
 - NPC Outposts and Renegade ships \(excluding Renegade support fighters\) have an increased chance of spawning with Pandora Tuning.
 - Outposts with Pandora Tuning guarantee that all ships they produce inherit Pandora Tuning.

4. Main Plot

- Phanon Playthrough:
 - While allied, Phanon operates at 60% production speed.
 - This penalty is removed after joining the OCV.

- OCV Playthrough:
 - Phanon is more likely to deploy Jump Beacons in both its own sectors and Commonwealth sectors.
 - Upon joining:
 - You receive only one blueprint per ship class.
 - Your starting fleet is weaker.
 - Xenon and OCV fleet strength is reduced after joining.

Vanilla missions have been replaced by a new system. There are 15 procedural missions:

Patrol \(fight\): Hunt Xenon fleets in a given sector. The Xenon will appear only when your own ship or one of your fleet leaders enters the sector. Kills made by your forces or hired mercenaries grant credits and reputation; kills made by other forces do not.

Suppression \(fight\): Eliminate the leader of a nearby enemy military squadron. The target belongs to a Commonwealth faction that is hostile to or engaged in a Total War with the mission giver. Only the designated leader must be defeated. Rewards depend on the target ship.

Bait \(fight\): Capture a nearby abandoned miner to attract Kha'ak ships from deep space. Kills made by your forces or hired mercenaries grant credits and reputation. If you successfully protect the miner, you can keep it.

Defense \(fight\): The Xenon have built a nearby Jump Beacon and are targeting a station. Protect the station and destroy the beacon.

Provision \(trade\): Deliver requested wares to a station using any of your ships. The reward is based on the average price of the requested wares.

Acquisition \(trade\): AI factions sometimes send Tugs to claim abandoned ships. These ships may be used by their Outposts or offered for sale to you through this mission.

Deliveries \(trade\): Make several deliveries for a shady character. Be prepared to defend yourself, as some pirates may take an interest in your cargo.

Prospecting \(think\): Scan asteroids in a given sector. If you have already scanned every asteroid there, new asteroids will be created for the mission.

Collection \(think\): Find Artefacts scattered throughout the target sector or an adjacent sector and return them to the station that issued the mission. Artefacts appear as floating wares that cannot be collected by the AI.

Exploration \(think\): Deploy Advanced Satellites at the specified coordinates. An error margin of 5 km is allowed. You can use the Move to Coordinates command under Navigation to reach the required positions.

Rescue \(think\): Capture an abandoned ship and return it to its station with all passengers alive. If you succeed, you can keep the ship.

Police \(think\): Find a criminal and bring him to justice. If you succeed, you can keep his ship.

Intel \(fight\): Scan a station hostile to the mission giver to collect intelligence. Your ship must be completely stopped for the scan to progress, and only your personal ship can complete this mission. Local Police may detect and attack you during the scan.

VIP \(think\): Transport a passenger to a nearby factory. Upon completion, the factory receives a temporary production bonus. You must be docked to accept this mission.

Supplies \(trade\): Deliver resources to a nearby factory for a custom production order. The order does not affect the station offering the mission, but the target factory will consume the resources you deliver. You must be docked to accept this mission.

To view a mission briefing offered by a station, dock at the station, use the Mission Briefing command under Additional Ship Commands, or open Personal Console -> Personal Journal. From the briefing, you can accept the mission or abandon it if you previously accepted it.

Some missions require you to dock at the offering station before you can view their briefing. The Mission Briefing command can otherwise be used from any of your ships.

Missions are generated periodically and have no time limit once accepted. Unaccepted missions will eventually expire.

Sectors, stations, wares, and entire factions can be blacklisted through a dedicated menu in your Personal Console. Blacklisted targets are ignored by most of your ships.\n\nYour ships normally use safe paths through the galaxy, avoiding hostile sectors such as those owned by the Xenon. You can choose whether ships are allowed to pass through blacklisted sectors when necessary. By default, blacklisted sectors are treated as hostile and avoided whenever an alternative route is available.

In Mayhem 3, formations, squadrons, and fleets follow the same basic rules:

1. Leader
The leader is at the center of the formation and controls its overall behavior.

2. Followers
Followers are the other ships in the formation. They prioritize protecting the leader, then attack the leader's target or assist other followers.

3. Support Ships
Support ships are fighters carried by a follower. While their carrier is alive, they operate independently from the rest of the formation and prioritize protecting and assisting their carrier. If the carrier is destroyed, its support ships rejoin the formation as standard followers. If the carrier is equipped with a Carrier Repair Module, damaged support ships remain docked while their hull is repaired.

Wings and turret scripts are among the few vanilla systems left largely unchanged.

All ships are repaired over time for free while docked at any Outpost. Ships can also be repaired aboard a carrier equipped with a Carrier Repair Module, although the process is slower than at an Outpost.

A carrier equipped with a Carrier Repair Module can also repair spaceborne followers under the following conditions:

- The carrier must be a capital ship with a hangar.
- The follower must not be docked.
- The follower must be part of the fleet.
- Neither the carrier nor the follower can be attacking.
- The follower must be an M6, TM, M8, or capital ship.

Stations automatically repair themselves over time.

Many equipment upgrades are installed on ships by default. However, equipment such as the Docking Computer and Transporter Device must be installed through Upgrade Ship in an Outpost's Hangar and require colored crystals. Colored crystals can be obtained through mining or transmuted from normal Crystals produced by Crystal Fabs.\n\nSee the Ship Equipment section of the encyclopedia for more information about the available equipment.

In Mayhem, lasers do not consume energy. Out-of-sector combat does not simulate laser energy consumption, effectively giving ships unlimited laser energy. To eliminate this imbalance between in-sector and out-of-sector combat, laser energy consumption is disabled entirely.

Fight Loot Chance \(FLC\) is a Litcube's Universe mechanic that determines the chance for a destroyed ship to drop installed wares. In Mayhem, FLC uses a fixed universal rate that applies to all ships, including your own. Ships attacked by your personal ship have twice the normal chance to drop loot. The FLC level displayed in the Pilot Status screen can therefore be ignored. Freighters are an exception: if they are carrying cargo when destroyed, they always drop it.\n\nMayhem uses its own bailing system. Abandoned ships are limited in number, making them less common than in Litcube's Universe.

Jump Points include your Jump Beacons and Jump Stations. Together, they form your personal gate network across the galaxy.

You are the only faction capable of crafting and deploying Jump Beacons. However, Phanon can use your Jump Points for travel. If you join the OCV, Phanon may also rebuild and operate their own Jump Beacon network.


Jump Beacons

To construct a Jump Beacon:
1. Build a Jumpdrive Core Factory at one of your Outposts.
2. Deploy the factory and have it produce Jumpdrive Cores.
3. Manufacture a Jump Beacon:
 - At an Outpost for twice the Mobile Factory production cost, or
 - From a ship equipped with a Mobile Factory Kit \(Special -> Manufacture command\)

Jump Beacons function like gates. When at least two are active, your ships will automatically route through them and seek the shortest available path. You can travel through your Jump Beacons manually using the custom hotkey.


Jump Stations

Outposts can unlock the Jump Station perk at the cost of 1 Jump Beacon and 1 Black Crystal. Jump Stations function identically to Jump Beacons for travel but are more secure.

Jump Stations can unlock the Jump Hole Generator perk for an upfront cost of 2 Black Crystals. Opening Jump Holes costs 1 Jump Beacon, 10 Red Crystals, 5 Yellow Crystals, 1 Blue Crystal, and 10,000 Energy Cells. Jump Holes are temporary gates that connect two otherwise distant sectors, allowing ships to travel directly between them while the connection remains active.


Jump Point Limits

There is a galaxy-wide limit on the number of active Jump Points. This limit depends on galaxy size and is reduced on Insane difficulty.


Beacon Security

Jump Beacons are vulnerable to hostile interference.

Xenon forces may infect a Jump Beacon. Once converted, the Beacon becomes a Xenon-controlled spawn point. Infection is irreversible. If you have joined the OCV, your ships will not oppose the conversion.

NPC factions may destroy enemy Jump Beacons in their territory. Pirates may target Beacons regardless of ownership; however, if you have joined the OCV, pirates will instead target only player-owned and Xenon Jump Beacons.

Jump Stations are immune to infection and cannot be destroyed in this manner.


Placement and Maintenance

The following placement and maintenance restrictions apply only on Hard and Insane difficulties:

To capture, place, or maintain a Jump Beacon, one of the following must be true:
- You own the sector.
- You are a close ally of the sector's faction.
 - Being a close ally requires reputation rank 6 \(7 on Insane\) or higher.
- The sector is unclaimed.
 - If this is the Renegades sector, the Renegades plot must be completed.

You cannot place or capture Jump Beacons in enemy sectors or in faction sectors where your reputation is insufficient.


Abandoned Jump Beacons

Abandoned Jump Beacons can be found in Terran Memory sectors. Higher difficulty levels reduce the number of abandoned Beacons.

Private companies employ both Traders and mercenaries. During their normal routine, mercenaries roam the galaxy and assist where needed. Some may attempt to smuggle illegal wares between factions. If you encounter a smuggler while holding a Police License, they will turn hostile as Pirates, allowing you to collect a bounty by destroying them.

Mercenaries can also be hired to escort your assets. Hiring one requires an initial fee equivalent to one hour of service, followed by a regular fee. Mercenaries can be dismissed at any time, although dismissing one within the first hour wastes part of the initial hiring fee. Some mercenaries may already have a client; hiring them costs more because they must be convinced to break their existing contract.

Nomad mercenaries spawn from the Nomad Flagship. They are cheaper to hire but may eventually leave your service. Infamy gained through piracy, such as destroying Company Traders or boarding ships, greatly reduces their chance of leaving.

Pirates have always hidden in the darkest corners of the universe, even before the Terrans' failed terraforming attempts. Pirate Bases can be found randomly in unclaimed sectors. They produce fighters, corvettes, and military transports that hunt down freighters and their cargo.\n\nPirate Bases respawn over time. However, they will stop respawning if no Pirate Bases or Yaki Outposts remain in the galaxy. You can dock at a Pirate Base even if it appears hostile, unless you have recently destroyed one. Pirate Bases can also be used to improve your reputation with a faction.
Periodically, Kha'ak ships emerge from deep space and raid the empire that controls the most stations in the galaxy.

Renegades are an unknown faction that specializes in fast hit-and-run raids against your empire. No one knows who hired them, but their objective is clear: harass your logistics, weaken your defenses, and force you to respond on their terms.

There are three main types of Renegade ships: roamers, assassins, and defenders. All three can transition into raiding behavior and attack your sectors.


Roamers

Roamers are the first Renegade ships you will encounter. Early on, they patrol distant sectors, targeting your satellites and vulnerable ships. If successful, they may accelerate to escape and flee toward a station. As your campaign progresses, either because too many roamers are active or your fleet power becomes high enough, new roamers will begin raiding your sectors directly.

Destroying a roamer yields a crate containing random crystals. The first 10 roamers you destroy also provide information about the Renegades. The first roamer you destroy begins the Renegades plot and reveals the sector containing the hidden gate. Subsequent roamer kills can drop gate code fragments required to unlock the gate to their home sector. Pirate ships have a small chance to provide hints about the Renegades, but they never drop gate code fragments.

Once you have collected all three gate code fragments, travel to the sector mentioned in the first clue and scan the special shipwreck. The gate code fragments are displayed with dashes for readability. Enter the code and solve the puzzle.

Success opens the gate to the Renegade home sector. Failure triggers immediate retaliation.


Assassins

Assassins appear if you fail the puzzle. They spawn near you and aggressively engage nearby assets. If they achieve their objective, they escalate into raids against your sectors.


Defenders

Defenders reside in the Renegade home sector and serve two purposes:

1. Territorial defense: they protect the Renegade station and surrounding space.

2. Invasion pressure: if you unlock the gate without establishing clear fleet superiority in their home sector, the Renegades may launch an invasion using their defenders as the strike force.


Scaling and Difficulty

Renegade spawns and ship composition scale with game difficulty and your fleet power. Higher difficulties and greater fleet power lead to more Renegade activity and tougher ship classes.

Destroying the Renegade station in their home sector completes the Renegades plot and awards generous rewards.

The Xenon are the unfortunate consequence of the Terrans' terraforming program centuries ago. They occupy several heavily defended sectors and gradually reinforce their territory with additional garrison fleets. They can also launch invasion fleets into the rest of the galaxy.

The OCV are an advanced branch of the same Terraformer network. They operate from the Maelstrom within Xenon territory and serve a more offensive role. OCV forces gather near the Maelstrom and periodically organize into powerful invasion fleets, while the Xenon provide most of the Terraformers' territorial defenses.

Xenon invaders prioritize capturing your Jump Beacons after spawning from their stations. Once captured, the Xenon can use these Beacons as spawn points.

A storyline allows you to join the OCV or work with Phanon, a defective branch of Terraformers. Joining the OCV provides significant benefits but also presents its own challenges.
